llmops-vs-mlops.explain:
## What it is

**MLOps** operationalises models you train: data pipelines, training runs, a model registry, deployment and drift monitoring. **LLMOps** inherits that discipline but most teams no longer train the model; they call a hosted one and build prompts, retrieval and tools around it.

What changes:
- The artefact you ship is a *bundle* (prompt, model id, retriever config, tools), not one weights file.
- Evaluation is fuzzy: outputs are free text, so you need LLM judges, rubrics and human review, not just accuracy.
- Cost is per token and latency is per request, so spend and tail latency become first-class operational metrics.
- Failure modes are new: hallucination, prompt injection, provider outages and silent model updates.

What stays the same: version control, CI, staged rollout, monitoring, rollback, incident review.

Interview angle: say that LLMOps is MLOps with a different unit of change and a harder evaluation problem, not a replacement.

LLMOps is the operating system around a bundle you did not train: prompts, pins, retrieval, tools, evals, and the service. MLOps habits stay; the unit of change is what flips.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: LLMOps vs MLOps. Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, lLMOps vs MLOps is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Monday quality drops with no app deploy are normal if aliases, prompts, or indexes can move. You need names for those movers.

The concrete requirement is: Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, they ask how LLMOps differs from MLOps. Say bundle versus weights, fuzzy eval, per-token cost, then list CI and rollback as the inherited spine. A strong answer names this item (LLMOps vs MLOps) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “LLMOps vs MLOps” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps.

Draw two columns (inherited vs new). Inherited: versions, CI, staging, rollback. New: prompt labels, model pins, index ids, judges, token budgets. Put every control in one column.

A support bot calls a hosted API. You pin a snapshot, store prompt v12, log k and chunk size, and fail CI when faithfulness drops. That is application LLMOps on a real app, not a new model lab.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-1: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “LLMOps vs MLOps” because the happy path works.** Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps. Renaming the team without a gate or a pin.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Versioning only weights while prompts live in a dashboard.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement llmops vs mlops. Treating HTTP 200 as quality.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

LLMOps vs MLOps: Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps. Different unit of change, same operating spine, plus pins and evals because the vendor can move. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-1. A reviewer asks you to prove “LLMOps vs MLOps.” You show Friday’s manifest (pin, prompt, index) and Monday’s alias move. Re-pin, re-run the set, quality returns. The artefact is the manifest, not a slide titled LLMOps.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need llmops vs mlops?” If they say it is only a new name, show an incident with no git change. If they ask about GPUs, split application vs model layers. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Traces with a complete bundle id, eval-gate fail rate, time-to-rollback for a prompt or pin. Also: time since you last exercised “LLMOps vs MLOps” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.

why-llm-systems-are-hard-to-operate.explain:
## What it is

LLM systems break the assumptions of ordinary services.

- **Non-determinism**: the same input can give different outputs, so tests that compare exact strings flake.
- **Quality is not an HTTP status**: a 200 response can be a hallucination. Health must be measured on content.
- **Silent upstream change**: a provider can update or deprecate a model and behaviour shifts without a deploy on your side.
- **Variable cost and latency**: cost scales with tokens; latency with output length and provider load; a single agent loop can burn money.
- **Untrusted inputs**: prompt injection means user and retrieved text can steer behaviour.
- **Many coupled parts**: prompt, retriever, chunking, tools and model interact, so one change moves several metrics.

Mitigation pattern: pin versions, trace everything, gate releases on evals, add runtime guardrails and budget limits, and monitor quality online.

LLMOps is the operating system around a bundle you did not train: prompts, pins, retrieval, tools, evals, and the service. MLOps habits stay; the unit of change is what flips.

what-a-release-consists-of.explain:
## What it is

A release of an LLM app is not just code. It is a **bundle of versioned parts**:

1. Application code (container image tag).
2. Prompts and templates (registry version or label).
3. Model id and parameters (pinned model, temperature, max tokens).
4. Retrieval setup: embedding model, chunking, index version, top-k, reranker.
5. Tool definitions and guardrail/policy configs.
6. Eval set version and the scores the bundle achieved.

Changing any one can change behaviour, so each needs a version and a record of which versions were live together. Write a **release manifest** (for example a JSON file with the commit SHA, prompt version, model id and index id) and log it on every trace.

**Agents** loop: the model chooses tools, observes results, and repeats. ## What it is

The level walks one app from laptop to production in a loop:

1. **Prepare**: config, pinned versions, tracing, an eval set.
2. **Track**: experiments and a prompt registry give every change a version and a score.
3. **Gate**: evals run in CI and block regressions.
4. **Protect**: runtime guardrails and limits.
5. **Package and serve**: FastAPI, streaming, Docker.
6. **Ship**: GitHub Actions builds commit-tagged images and deploys with approval.
7. **Run on AWS**: EC2/IAM, secrets, blue/green, autoscaling.
8. **Observe**: metrics, dashboards, alerts, Langfuse traces, online evals.
9. **Respond and improve**: incidents, runbooks, and failures fed back into the eval suite.

what-is-non-deterministic-in-the-loop.explain:
## What it is

Three moving parts in an LLM system are **non-deterministic unless you pin and record them**: the **prompt** (and anything it includes), the **model** (sampling and vendor snapshots), and the **judge** you use to score outputs.

A prompt edited in place is a silent behaviour change. A model alias or temperature > 0 makes replays diverge. A judge model that is itself unpinned can flip a gate from pass to fail without your product changing.

“Pin and record all three” means: version the prompt, pin the product model and its sampling, pin the judge model and rubric, and write those ids on the run and the trace. Determinism here is operational, not mathematical. You want replayable decisions, not identical poetry.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Gates that flake destroy trust. Teams disable the eval job. Then a real regression ships. Judges that move under you create fake regressions and fake wins.

Interviewers ask why your eval is red on re-run. If you cannot name prompt, product model, and judge pins, you do not yet operate the loop.

## How it works + one small example

On every offline run and every production trace store:

- `prompt_id` + hash of the rendered template
- `model_id` (snapshot, not `latest`) + temperature / seed policy
- `judge_id` + rubric version + judge temperature

Example. CI fails Friday. You replay with the same three pins and it fails the same way — a real regression. A second team replays with `judge=latest` and gets a pass. Their gate is a coin flip. You freeze the judge snapshot and the suite becomes a signal again.

Where sampling must stay on (creative copy), do not use exact match. Use a tolerance band, repeated trials, or a human step. Still pin the judge.

## Failure modes

1. **Pinned product, floating judge.** You “regressed” because the judge updated.

2. **Temperature 0 in CI, 0.7 in prod.** The gate never saw production noise.

3. **Prompt text logged but not versioned.** You can read it after the fact; you cannot roll it back by label.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prompts, product models, and judges all move. I pin and record all three on every run and trace. A flaky gate is usually an unpinned judge or a sampling mismatch, not “LLMs being random.”

## A concrete walk-through

The eval job is red, green, red. Product pin is stable. You find the judge alias moved twice in a week. You pin `judge-2026-03-01`, set judge temperature to 0, and store the rubric hash. The next ten runs agree. You add “judge pin” to the release manifest.

## Interview follow-up

They say “just use human eval.” Reply: humans are a stage, not a pin. I still record which rubric and which product bundle they scored, or I cannot compare months.

## What I would measure

Eval rerun agreement on a frozen bundle, share of runs with all three pins, and CI jobs skipped because “the judge is flaky.”
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “what is non deterministic in the loop” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

A floating judge creates fake regressions.

Replayability is the goal, not identical tokens every time.

questions.a: The prompt (id and rendered hash), the product model snapshot and sampling, and the judge model plus rubric. Missing any one makes reruns incomparable.

questions.a: Whether the judge pin or temperature moved, then whether the product model alias moved, then whether the prompt label is stable. Freeze the judge before you rewrite tests.

questions.a: The gate never sees the noise users see. Either run the gate with production sampling and a band, or keep prod at the gated settings for that task.

questions.a: Prompt id and rendered hash, model pin and sampling, retrieval ids, and if a judge scored it, the judge pin and rubric version.

questions.q: Does pinning make the model deterministic?
questions.a: No. It makes the decision loop replayable enough to trust a gate. Residual sampling may remain; you handle that with bands, repeats, or humans.

human-review-as-an-llmops-stage.explain:
## What it is

Not every change is a silent deploy. **Human review** is an LLMOps stage: a person looks at a prompt, a model pin, a policy change, or a sample of outputs before that change can reach all users.

Automation still runs — unit tests, eval gate, schema checks — but some deltas have no trustworthy automatic score yet: a new refusal policy, a tone change, a tool that can write, a judge you do not trust on a new domain. Those get a reviewer, a checklist, and a recorded decision.

This is not “we look at a notebook sometimes.” It is a required step with an owner, like a production approval in CI, or a sampled review queue with an SLA.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Silent deploys of prompts are how brand and legal incidents happen. The model is fluent; the new wording promises a refund you do not offer. A gate on last month’s golden set will not catch a new claim.

Interviewers ask who can change the system prompt. “Anyone with the dashboard password” is a fail. “A labelled version, a gate, and a human approval for policy-touching prompts” is a pass.

## How it works + one small example

Split changes by risk.

- Low risk (typo in an example): gate + auto-promote to staging, human optional.
- Medium (retriever k, tone): gate + one reviewer.
- High (tools that write, legal wording, new model family): gate + named approver + canary.

Example. Marketing wants a friendlier prompt. You open a registry PR from `v12` to `v13`, run the suite (format still passes, a new “we’ll refund immediately” sentence appears in 8 of 50 cases). A reviewer blocks promotion, edits the wording, re-runs, and then moves `staging`. Production still needs the weekly sampled review, not a silent flip.

Record who approved, which sample they saw, and the prompt id. That is the audit trail.

## Failure modes

1. **Review with no artefact.** A Slack thumbs-up on unversioned text. You cannot replay what they approved.

2. **Review instead of a gate.** Humans are slow and miss regressions the suite would catch. Use both.

3. **Every change needs a VP.** The queue dies and people edit prod to bypass it. Risk-band the path.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Human review is a stage, not a vibe. Policy, write-tools, and new models get a named approver on a versioned artefact after the eval gate. I will not silent-deploy those, and I will not replace the gate with a Slack emoji.

## A concrete walk-through

A tool that emails customers is added. CI is green. You still require a reviewer to watch ten traces in staging, including one forced tool failure. They catch a “I have emailed them” lie when the tool 500s. You add that case to the suite and only then move `prod`.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if LLM-as-judge replaces humans. Say: it scales sampling; it does not approve a new legal sentence. I keep humans on policy and on a weekly sample the judge is not trusted to close.

## What I would measure

Share of production prompt/model changes with a recorded approver, time-in-review by risk band, and incidents where an unreviewed prompt reached users.

Humans approve versioned artefacts after the automated gate.

questions.a: Some changes — policy wording, write-tools, new model families — are not fully scored by the current suite. A recorded human decision on a versioned artefact stops silent deploys that create brand or legal incidents.

questions.a: On policy and write-path changes, and on a weekly sample used to audit the judge. The judge does not approve new legal claims by itself.

pinned-model-dependency-versions.explain:
## What it is

Reproducibility needs **pinning** on two fronts.

**Model**: use a dated or versioned model id where the provider offers one instead of a moving alias such as "latest". Aliases can change behaviour without any change on your side. Record the exact id on each trace. Plan upgrades as a deliberate release: run evals, compare, then switch. Also watch deprecation dates.

**Dependencies**: lock Python packages (lockfile with hashes if possible: `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock` or pinned `requirements.txt`), pin the base Docker image tag or digest, and pin the embedding model and index builder version since changing embeddings requires re-indexing.

Trade-off: pinning delays security and quality fixes, so schedule periodic upgrade PRs gated by the eval suite.

Failure mode: an unpinned library bump changes tokenisation or default parameters and quality drifts with no diff in your repo.

Preparation is boring on purpose: reuse the Level 4 and 5 apps, make behaviour configurable, pin versions, stamp request ids, and carry the Level 7 set as the yardstick.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Pinned model & dependency versions. Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, pinned model & dependency versions is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Inherited systems do not get a greenfield rewrite. You extract an entrypoint, a config object, and an eval command, then you operate.

The concrete requirement is: Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, production-ready means timeouts, versioned logs, an eval gate, rollback, and a budget cap — artefacts, not Docker as a personality. A strong answer names this item (Pinned model & dependency versions) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Pinned model & dependency versions” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today.

Inventory each app: entrypoint, literals to lift into config, missing pins, missing request id, eval command. Change one of those per PR.

You lift model, prompt ref, and k into YAML, add request_id at the HTTP edge, and run make eval against l7-gold@v8 before any Docker work.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-2: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “Pinned model & dependency versions” because the happy path works.** Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today. Building a third demo instead of operating the two you have.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Literals in three files so staging and prod disagree.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement pinned model & dependency versions. A gold set that moves whenever a prompt would fail.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Pinned model & dependency versions: Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today. Same apps, typed config, pins, traces from the first hop, Level 7 as the floor. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-2. A reviewer asks you to prove “Pinned model & dependency versions.” Laptop make eval and CI call the same target. A prompt flag flips back in one minute. Contract tests fail when a field becomes a string. That is prepared.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need pinned model & dependency versions?” They want a new agent. Refuse. They want latest models automatically. Nightly eval, then move a pin. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Levers changeable without a code commit, rebuild-to-rebuild eval delta, tickets that include a request id. Also: time since you last exercised “Pinned model & dependency versions” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.

- A request/trace id returned to the client and logged.
- Release identifiers: git SHA, prompt version, model id.

- Token counts, latency and errors per span.
- User or session id (hashed) and feedback when available.

Tools: OpenTelemetry-style spans, or LLM-specific platforms such as Langfuse or MLflow tracing, wired in via decorators or SDK callbacks.

## What it is

The **evaluation set** you built at Level 7 is the yardstick for every operational decision in this level: a curated set of inputs with expected answers, reference contexts or rubrics, covering typical cases, edge cases and known failures.

Used as:
- **Baseline**: score the current release before changing anything.
- **Gate**: CI fails if metrics fall below thresholds.
- **Comparator**: A/B a new prompt or model against the baseline on the same cases.
- **Regression log**: production failures are appended.

Properties of a good set: representative of real traffic, labelled or rubric-scored, versioned like code, split into a fast subset and a full suite, and reviewed by a human.

Caveat: a static set goes stale and can be overfit by prompt tuning. Refresh it from production samples and keep a held-out portion you do not tune against.

Preparation is boring on purpose: reuse the Level 4 and 5 apps, make behaviour configurable, pin versions, stamp request ids, and carry the Level 7 set as the yardstick.

feature-flags-on-prompts.explain:
## What it is

A **feature flag on a prompt** lets you choose which prompt version a request uses without rebuilding the image. Typical shape: flag `prompt_support` → `v12` or `v13`, possibly by tenant, percentage, or internal user.

Flags are how you canary and how you **flip back without a rebuild**. They are not a substitute for versioning: the flag points at a registry id. If the flag stores raw prompt text, you are back to untracked edits.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Prompt regressions should take seconds to undo, not a Docker rebuild and a deploy window. Interviewers ask how you would stop a bad wording at 2 a.m. The senior answer is “move the flag to the last good label,” not “hotfix the container.”

## How it works + one small example

Resolve the prompt id at request start from a flag service or config, fetch that version (with a pinned fallback), and stamp the id on the trace.

Example. You set `prompt_support=v13` for 5 percent of traffic. Online eval and spend look fine for two hours. You raise to 50 percent, then 100 percent. At 40 percent faithfulness dips. You set the flag back to `v12`. No image moved. The rollback is the flag.

Guard the flag: only known registry ids, default deny to the last production label if the flag service is down.

## Failure modes

1. **Flag holds raw text.** You have reinvented the unversioned dashboard.

2. **Flag without a fallback.** Flag service outage becomes a prod outage.

3. **One flag for prompt and model.** You cannot roll back only the wording.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prompt flags point at versioned labels so I can canary and flip back without a rebuild. The flag is a pointer, not a paste bin, and it fails to the last good label if the flag service dies.

## A concrete walk-through

You ship `v15` to 5 percent. Traces show a new refund promise. You flip the flag to `v14` in one minute. Later you delete `v15` from `prod` eligibility. The image tag never changed; the incident timeline still has prompt ids.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if flags replace CI. Say: no. Flags change who sees an already-built, already-gated version. A brand-new text still goes through the registry and the suite before the flag can point at it.

## What I would measure

Time to flip back a prompt, share of prompt rollbacks that needed no image deploy, and flag-service fallback hits.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “feature flags on prompts” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

A flag service outage must not take the product down: fail to the last good production label bundled in the image or still sitting in memory. Separate the prompt flag from the model-pin flag so you can revert wording without changing the snapshot. New text still passes the eval gate before any flag may point at it. Practise a 2 a.m. flip on staging until the motion is boring.

## Practise until it is boring

Rehearse feature flags on prompts until you can name the artefact, the metric, and the undo without notes. If you cannot drill it, assume the control is dead. Write the last date you exercised it next to the cheat-sheet line.
keyPoints: Flags select a prompt version; they do not store unversioned text.
Flip back without a rebuild is the reason they exist.
Canary by percentage or tenant, then raise or revert.
Fail to the last good label if the flag service is down.
Do not bundle model pin and prompt on one flag.
New text still passes the eval gate before a flag can point at it.

questions.q: What does a feature flag on a prompt actually store?
questions.a: A pointer to a versioned prompt id or label, optionally with a percentage or tenant rule. Not the raw prompt text.

questions.q: A new prompt looks harmful at 5 percent. How do you stop it at 2 a.m.?
questions.a: Point the flag back at the last good label. Do not rebuild the image. Then record the ids in the incident note.

questions.q: The flag service is down and the app starts failing closed on every request. What was missing?
questions.a: A pinned local fallback to the last production prompt label so a flag outage is not a product outage.

questions.q: Why not put the model pin on the same flag as the prompt?
questions.a: You need to revert wording without changing the model, and the other way around. Separate levers, same gate.

questions.q: Where do flags sit relative to the eval gate?
questions.a: After. The version must already have passed the suite. The flag only chooses who receives that version.

contract-tests-on-the-output-schema.explain:
## What it is

**Contract tests on the output schema** treat the model’s structured output as an API. If a required field disappears, changes type, or violates an enum, the **build breaks** — before a caller in billing or the UI does.

This is narrower than a quality gate. Faithfulness can pass while `order_id` becomes a sentence. Schema tests are cheap, deterministic, and belong next to unit tests as well as inside the eval suite.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Downstream services parse JSON. A fluent, schema-breaking answer is an incident. Interviewers ask how you stop the model from dropping a field after a prompt tweak. “We have contract tests on the schema and we re-ask or fail the gate” is the engineering answer.

## How it works + one small example

Define the schema once (JSON Schema or a typed model). In CI, run a bag of fixtures — including adversarial ones — and assert parse + required fields + types. In runtime, validate and re-ask or fail closed.

Example. The ticket router must emit `{label, confidence, queue}`. A prompt “be more helpful” adds a `note` and drops `queue`. Contract tests fail on 40 of 40 fixtures. The quality judge might still have called the label fine. You never promote.

Keep the schema in the repo next to the prompt id that is supposed to satisfy it. A schema change is its own review.

## Failure modes

1. **Schema only in the system prompt.** The model “tries.” CI does not enforce.

2. **Optional everything.** The contract cannot fail, so it cannot protect callers.

3. **Breaking the schema to pass a judge.** You shipped stringly types and called it quality.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Structured outputs are an API. I keep contract tests on the schema in CI so a missing field fails the build, and I validate again at runtime with a re-ask or a hard fail — not hope in a prompt.

## A concrete walk-through

A prompt change goes green on faithfulness and red on contract tests: `total_cents` is now `"12.50 USD"`. You refuse the promote, tighten the schema instruction, and add that fixture. Billing never sees the string.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if structured-output mode from the provider replaces tests. Say: it reduces breaks; I still test, because prompts, tools, and wrappers can bypass or wrap the field.

## What I would measure

Contract-test failures caught in CI versus in production parse errors, and time from schema change to fixture update.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “contract tests on the output schema” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

Keep the schema in the same review as the prompt version that is supposed to satisfy it. Provider structured-output modes reduce breaks; they do not replace fixtures, because wrappers and tools can still wrap a field as a sentence. Optional-everything schemas cannot fail and therefore cannot protect billing. Run the same fixtures in CI and again at runtime before a downstream parse.
keyPoints: Treat model JSON as an API with contract tests in CI.
A missing or mistyped field must break the build.
Quality judges can pass while the schema is already broken.
Validate again at runtime; re-ask or fail closed.
Keep schema and prompt version side by side.
Provider structured-output modes do not replace fixtures.

questions.q: What is a contract test on an LLM output schema?
questions.a: An automated check that parsed outputs still have the required fields and types. If a field disappears or changes type, CI fails even if the text looks good.

questions.q: Faithfulness is up but the billing parser is throwing. What test was missing?
questions.a: A schema contract on fields like amounts and ids. Add fixtures and fail the build when types drift.

questions.q: Where should schema contracts run besides CI?
questions.a: At runtime on every response: validate, re-ask once, then fail closed or route to a human — do not send broken JSON downstream.

questions.q: Why not make every field optional to keep tests green?
questions.a: Then the contract cannot fail and callers still break. Required fields are the point of the contract.

questions.q: A provider offers structured outputs. Why keep fixtures?
questions.a: Prompts, wrappers, and tools can still emit the wrong shape. Fixtures lock the contract you promised to callers.

interview.explain:
## What it is

When someone asks what **production-ready** means for an LLM app, give a checklist, not a vendor name: **timeouts**, **logs** (with request ids and versions), an **eval gate**, a **rollback**, and a **budget cap**.

That list is the interview line for this module. It maps to real artefacts: request and model timeouts plus disconnect handling; traces that carry the bundle; CI that runs the Level 7 yardstick; a way to move a prompt label or a known image tag back; a per-request and daily spend cap so a loop cannot empty the account.

If you cannot point at each artefact, you are not production-ready. A streaming UI alone is a demo.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the question you will actually get. Hiring managers have been burned by demos. They listen for whether you mention quality gates and money, or only Docker. On the job the same list is how you push back on “just ship it.”

## How it works + one small example

Answer in thirty seconds, then offer evidence.

“Production-ready means every call has timeouts, every request is logged with prompt and model versions, no change lands without the eval gate, I can roll back a prompt or an image without a rebuild, and spend is capped per request and per day.”

Example evidence: a CI log where a broken prompt failed the gate; a flag flip that restored `v12`; a trace with `req_…` and pins; a config field `spend_cap_usd=0.25`; a 15s model timeout that cancelled a disconnect.

If they press on observability, add online samples. If they press on security, add guardrails. Do not drop the five.

## Failure modes

1. **Listing tools instead of properties.** “We use Langfuse” is not timeouts or a cap.

2. **Rollback of only the container.** They will ask about the prompt.

3. **No number on the budget.** “We watch spend” is not a cap.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Production-ready means timeouts, versioned logs, an eval gate, a rollback that includes the prompt id, and a hard budget cap. If I cannot show each artefact, I will call it a demo.

## A concrete walk-through

You are asked “is it prod ready?” on a panel. You draw five boxes, attach one artefact to each, and mention the last time the gate blocked you. The panel stops asking about Kubernetes.

## Interview follow-up

They add “what about scale?” Reply: scale comes after this list. An uncapped, un-gated, un-traced service that scales will only fail louder.

## What I would measure

experiments-in-mlflow.explain:
## What it is

**MLflow Tracking** organises work into **experiments** (a named group, e.g. `rag-prompt-tuning`) containing **runs** (one attempt). Each run records parameters, metrics, tags and artifacts.

For LLM apps a run is one evaluation of one configuration over the eval set:
- params: model id, temperature, top-k, chunk size, prompt version
- metrics: faithfulness, answer relevance, latency p95, cost per query
- artifacts: the prompt text, outputs file, eval report

Minimal pattern: `with mlflow.start_run(): mlflow.log_params(cfg); mlflow.log_metrics(scores)`.

Why: without it, results live in notebooks and memory, and nobody can say which setting produced the good number. Failure modes: logging too little (cannot reproduce), mixing unrelated experiments in one bucket, or not tagging the git SHA.

Tracking is MLflow runs plus a prompt registry with labels. Parameters, metrics, and artefacts make a run comparable. Labels make wording releasable without a rebuild.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Experiments in MLflow. Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, experiments in MLflow is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. “k=8 was better” is folklore unless it is a run with the rest of the bundle and a gold-set id.

The concrete requirement is: Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, they want how you version prompts and how you compare experiments. Registry labels plus a fair comparison table is the answer. A strong answer names this item (Experiments in MLflow) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Experiments in MLflow” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set.

Baseline both apps. One change per run. Log params, scores, prompt file, samples. Promote staging→prod by moving a label after the same eval command.

Four runs: chunk 400/800 × k 4/8. You keep k=4 when the faithfulness gain is 0.01 and tokens jump 40 percent. The losing cells stay in MLflow.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-3: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “Experiments in MLflow” because the happy path works.** Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set. One run for an afternoon of tweaks.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Editing live prompt text in place.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement experiments in mlflow. Comparing runs that sat different exams.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Experiments in MLflow: Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set. Every attempt is a run; every wording is a version; promotion is a label move after the same command. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-3. A reviewer asks you to prove “Experiments in MLflow.” You open the baseline run, compare a candidate, reject a friendlier 20-row set, move production back from v19 to v18 when traces group on v19.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need experiments in mlflow?” Spreadsheets until two people must replay. Then you need run ids and artefacts. Registry outage: cache plus baked fallback. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Releases that cite a run id and evalset tag, time to label-rollback, requests served from prompt fallback. Also: time since you last exercised “Experiments in MLflow” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.

3. If gates pass, move `production` to v12.

dataset-versioning.explain:
## What it is

The **golden set is as important as the prompt**. Version it (`l7-gold@v8`), store it as an artefact, and record which version a run and a release used. A prompt `v14` that “scored 0.9” on an unnamed set is an advertisement.

Dataset versioning includes the cases, the labels or rubrics, and the split (fast subset vs full). Changing a label on one case without a version bump rewrites history.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

People obsess over prompt versions and treat the exam as clay. That is how gates get quieter. Interviewers ask how you know a year-old score is comparable. “Same dataset version and judge pin” is the answer.

## How it works + one small example

Keep the set in git or object storage with a semver or date id. MLflow run tags `evalset=…`. CI checks out that id. Adding a case is a reviewed PR that bumps the id and, if needed, re-scores the baseline.

Example. You add six production misses. That is `v9`. You re-run the current production bundle and the candidate prompt on `v9`. You do not claim `v14` beat `v8`’s 0.86 on a different exam.

## Failure modes

1. **Editing labels in place** to make a favourite prompt win.

2. **No id in CI** — the runner clones `main` and the set moved.

3. **Prompt registry with a folder of anonymous JSONL.** One side is versioned; the exam is not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I version the golden set like a prompt. Every score names the dataset id, and I will not compare runs that sat different exams. Adding a miss bumps the version and re-scores the baseline.

## A concrete walk-through

A PM quotes “0.92 on eval.” You ask “which dataset version?” They do not know. You show two runs: 0.92 on a 15-row demo, 0.71 on `l7-gold@v8`. The meeting uses `v8` from then on.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if the set should live in the prompt registry. Say: it can live anywhere addressable. The requirement is an id on the run, not a particular SaaS.

## What I would measure

Runs missing `evalset` tags, and baseline re-scores after each dataset bump.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “dataset versioning” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

A 15-row demo set is not the golden set. CI must pin the set id rather than cloning whatever happens to be on main. When you add production misses, bump the version and re-score the current production bundle so the new floor is honest. Editing a label in place to pass a favourite prompt is a process incident, not a data cleanup.

## Practise until it is boring

Rehearse dataset versioning until you can name the artefact, the metric, and the undo without notes. If you cannot drill it, assume the control is dead. Write the last date you exercised it next to the cheat-sheet line.

Write the artefact path on a card. Open it once a week. If the path is stale, the control is stale. That weekly open is the cheapest drill that keeps this item honest.

## What it is

**Promotion rules** are the same **eval command** from **dev to staging to prod**. What changes is who must approve and how much traffic you expose — not the exam, not the judge pin, and not a “prod-only” notebook.

Dev can be the fast subset. Staging is the full suite plus a human if the risk band says so. Prod is a label move or a deploy of a bundle that already passed that command.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

the-eval-suite-as-deepeval-tests.explain:
## What it is

**DeepEval** lets you write LLM evaluations as ordinary pytest tests. Each case is an `LLMTestCase` (input, actual output, expected output, retrieval context), asserted with `assert_test(test_case, [metrics])`, so the suite runs with `pytest` or `deepeval test run` and fails with a non-zero exit code, which is exactly what CI needs.

Structure:
- A dataset of cases loaded from versioned files.
- A function that calls your real pipeline to get actual outputs and contexts.
- Metrics with thresholds (see below) applied per case.

Why this form: it reuses test tooling (fixtures, markers, parametrisation, reports) and makes quality a merge condition. Cost: judge-based metrics call an LLM, so tests are slower and cost tokens; keep the number of cases and metrics deliberate. Check current DeepEval docs for API details.

The Level 7 suite becomes automated tests (DeepEval or equivalent) in an ordinary runner. RAG and agent get different metrics and thresholds versus the baseline. The gate sees prompt, model, and retrieval changes as first-class.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: The eval suite as DeepEval tests. Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the eval suite as DeepEval tests is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A build that only lints will ship a polite regression. The gate is how you refuse it.

The concrete requirement is: Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, they ask how you stop a bad prompt. “It fails CI on faithfulness versus baseline” is the line, then canary and shadow. A strong answer names this item (The eval suite as DeepEval tests) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “The eval suite as DeepEval tests” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner.

Wrap the suite as tests. Set per-metric floors with a small band. Fast subset on every commit, full suite before release. Log the gated run in MLflow. Canary a prompt; shadow a model.

A wording change drops faithfulness 0.06 and passes unit tests. CI goes red. You never build the image. A later model pin is shadowed on live traffic and scored without users seeing it.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-4: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “The eval suite as DeepEval tests” because the happy path works.** Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner. Exact-string tests on sampled outputs that the team then skips.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. A friendlier exam to pass a favourite prompt.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement the eval suite as deepeval tests. Gating code but not prompt or pin changes.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The eval suite as DeepEval tests: Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner. Same suite, per-metric floors, prompt and model in the gate, canary before a full flip, shadow before users see a new pin. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-4. A reviewer asks you to prove “The eval suite as DeepEval tests.” You commit a broken prompt on purpose. Actions fails on the eval job. You revert. Then you canary 5 percent, watch cost and quality, and flip back from the flag — still no image rebuild.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need the eval suite as deepeval tests?” Non-determinism: pin sampling, repeat, use a band. Cost of the full suite: subset first, full before release. Shadow is not a substitute for the offline set. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Gate blocks per week, promotions that skipped the full suite, canaries that flipped back. Also: time since you last exercised “The eval suite as DeepEval tests” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.

## What it is

A gate needs a **pass threshold per metric**, set from data, not guessed. Different metrics deserve different bars: faithfulness for a medical app may need 0.9, answer relevancy 0.7.

1. Score the baseline several times to see level and noise.
2. Set the threshold slightly below baseline (leave room for noise) for existing behaviour, or higher for safety-critical metrics.
3. Review failing cases at the boundary to check the bar is meaningful.
4. Ratchet up as quality improves; never lower silently.

Two styles: an *absolute* floor per case, and an *aggregate* rule (for example mean above X and no more than N failing cases). Hard-fail critical categories (safety, PII) at 100%.

handling-non-determinism.explain:
## What it is

LLM outputs vary run to run, and LLM judges vary too, so a single run can pass or fail by chance and create **flaky gates**.

Techniques:
- Lower **temperature** (and set a seed where the provider supports it) for eval runs; this reduces but does not remove variance.
- Evaluate **semantic properties** (grounded, relevant, correct fact) rather than exact string match.
- **Repeat** borderline cases (for example 3 runs) and use the mean or majority.
- Use **aggregate thresholds** over many cases so single flips wash out.
- Keep the judge model and prompt pinned.
- Measure the suite's own noise by running the baseline repeatedly.

Trade-off: repeats multiply cost and time. Spend them where cases are close to the threshold.

The Level 7 suite becomes automated tests (DeepEval or equivalent) in an ordinary runner. RAG and agent get different metrics and thresholds versus the baseline. The gate sees prompt, model, and retrieval changes as first-class.

## What it is

**NeMo Guardrails** (NVIDIA, open source) adds programmable rails around an LLM app. Rails are defined in config using the Colang language plus YAML: you describe user intents with example utterances and the allowed flows.

Rail types:
- **Input rails** check or modify user messages.
- **Dialog / topical rails** keep the bot on-topic, for instance refusing questions outside banking support.

## What it is

**Streamlit** gives a quick Python UI for demos and internal tools: `st.chat_input`, `st.chat_message` and session state for history. Keep it **thin**: the frontend only collects input, calls the backend API and renders results. No model keys, retrieval logic or prompts in the UI process.

Benefits: one place for logic (the API), the same API serves other clients, the UI can be replaced, and secrets stay server-side. The frontend talks to the backend URL from configuration (in Docker Compose, the service name).

tests-eval-gate-build.explain:
## What it is

A pipeline orders checks from cheap to expensive and stops at the first failure ("fail fast").

1. **Lint and unit tests**: seconds; no LLM calls (mock the provider).
2. **Eval gate**: run the smoke eval subset (DeepEval/pytest) against the real pipeline and compare with thresholds; log to MLflow. This is the LLM-specific stage.
3. **Build**: build the Docker image only if previous stages pass.
4. **Push** to the registry, then **deploy** (staging, then production).

In GitHub Actions, express order with `needs:` between jobs. Use path filters so prompt/config changes trigger the eval job too. Cache dependencies. Keep the full eval suite for merges to main or pre-release, and the smoke subset for PRs.

Concerns: eval jobs spend provider money, so limit them to relevant changes and cap spend; secrets for the provider must not be exposed to PRs from forks. Failure mode: building and deploying in parallel with tests, so a failing eval cannot stop the release.

CI is tests, then the eval gate, then an image tagged with the commit, pushed only if the gate passed. Secrets via OIDC or Actions secrets, never logs. Staging auto, prod manual. Rollback is a known tag.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Tests → eval gate → build. Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, tests → eval gate → build is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A notebook eval that someone remembers to run is not a required check. Fork PRs must not see provider keys.

The concrete requirement is: Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, your CI for an LLM app is lint, unit, eval gate, then deploy the pin — in that order. A strong answer names this item (Tests → eval gate → build) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Tests → eval gate → build” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order.

Workflow: unit → eval → build → push tag=gitsha. OIDC to the cloud; no long-lived keys in logs. Environment protection for production. Keep the previous tag deployable.

A prompt PR fails eval and never publishes an image. A main build publishes app:a1b2. Prod waits for approval. Rollback is CodeDeploy of app:9c0d, not a rebuild.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-7: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “Tests → eval gate → build” because the happy path works.** Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order. Building the image before the gate.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Printing secrets in action output.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement tests → eval gate → build. Rollback that requires compiling last week’s laptop.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Tests → eval gate → build: Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order. Required eval, commit-tagged images, OIDC secrets, manual prod, rollback to a known tag. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-7. A reviewer asks you to prove “Tests → eval gate → build.” You open Actions: red eval job, no push. Then a green run, tag in the registry, staging auto, prod waiting. You deploy the previous tag in a drill.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need tests → eval gate → build?” Forks: no secrets, no eval that spends money, or use a dummy. OIDC: the cloud trusts GitHub’s token; you do not paste AWS keys into YAML. - Traceability from a running instance (`/version`) to a commit, eval run and prompt version.

manual-approval-for-production.explain:
## What it is

## What it is

**EC2** runs your container host. An **IAM role** attached to the instance (via an instance profile) gives applications on it temporary AWS credentials automatically from the metadata service, so no access keys sit on disk.

Typical permissions for this app: pull images from ECR, read specific secrets from Secrets Manager, write logs/metrics to CloudWatch, and let CodeDeploy fetch artefacts from S3.

Practice:
- **Least privilege**: allow only named resources and actions.
- Require **IMDSv2** to reduce SSRF-based credential theft.
- Place instances in private subnets behind a load balancer; use security groups to allow only the load balancer to reach the app port.
- Use patched AMIs and manage via SSM instead of SSH where possible.

Failure modes: an over-broad `*` policy, access keys copied onto the instance, and an app vulnerable to SSRF that can reach the metadata endpoint.

AWS deploy: EC2 with an instance role, secrets from Secrets Manager, CodeDeploy pulling a tagged image, in-place or blue/green with health checks, an ALB whose idle timeout survives SSE, ASGs that scale on concurrency, and a rollback that includes the prompt id.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: EC2 with an IAM role. Provision EC2 instances for the application, install Docker, and attach an IAM role instead of storing access keys on the machine.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, eC2 with an IAM role is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Access keys on the box and a 60s ALB timeout will fail a streaming LLM app in boring ways.

The concrete requirement is: Provision EC2 instances for the application, install Docker, and attach an IAM role instead of storing access keys on the machine. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, they want IAM roles, secrets not on disk, health-gated deploys, and the sentence that reverting the container is not enough. A strong answer names this item (EC2 with an IAM role) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “EC2 with an IAM role” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Provision EC2 instances for the application, install Docker, and attach an IAM role instead of storing access keys on the machine.

Role on the instance. Secrets at container start. CodeDeploy + health. Choose in-place vs blue/green. Raise ALB idle timeout. Scale on in-flight requests, not CPU. Respect provider rate limits. Incident notes without user text.

## What it is

**In-place**: stop the app on existing instances, install the new version, restart (often rolling across instances). Cheap, no extra capacity, but there is reduced capacity during the roll and rollback means reinstalling the old version.

## What it is

An **Application Load Balancer** has an **idle timeout** (default 60 seconds; check current docs) which closes connections with no data for that long. LLM requests can be silent for a while before the first token, especially for long contexts or agent steps, and a streamed response with long gaps can be cut.

- Raise the ALB idle timeout above your longest expected silence.
- Send **SSE keep-alive comments** (for example every 15 seconds).

- Disable response buffering at any reverse proxy.
- Set the target group deregistration delay to cover in-flight streams during deploys.

Failure mode: answers truncated at exactly 60 seconds, or intermittent 502/504 errors under load.

## What it is

An **Auto Scaling Group (ASG)** keeps a desired number of EC2 instances, launching from a **launch template** (AMI, instance type, role, user data) across availability zones and replacing unhealthy ones using load balancer health checks.

Settings: min, desired and max capacity; a scaling policy; **health check grace period** long enough for the app to boot and pull images; instance warm-up time so new instances are not counted in metrics prematurely; and cooldowns to avoid flapping.

Scaling in: use **connection draining / lifecycle hooks** so instances finish streams before termination, and scale-in protection during deployments if needed.

## What it is

LLM providers enforce **rate limits** on requests per minute and tokens per minute (and sometimes concurrency) per key/organisation. Your fleet shares them, so adding instances does not add capacity: it just reaches the cap sooner and produces **429** errors.

Implications:
- Know your limits and compute max sustainable throughput (tokens per minute / average tokens per request).
- Make scaling **bounded** by that cap (max ASG size).
- Add a shared **rate limiter / queue** in front of the provider, **retry with exponential backoff and jitter** on 429/5xx, and respect `Retry-After`.
- Shed load gracefully (clear error, queue, smaller model, cached answers) instead of timing out.
- Optionally fall back to a second provider or key pool, and request higher quotas ahead of launches.
- Monitor 429 rate and token usage against quota.

Failure mode: autoscaling out during an incident, amplifying retries and making the 429 storm worse.

## What it is

**Prometheus** is a time-series monitoring system that **pulls** (scrapes) metrics over HTTP from targets on an interval and stores them. **Node Exporter** is an agent exposing host metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) at `/metrics` on port 9100.

Concepts: a *metric* with *labels* (`http_requests_total{route="/chat",status="200"}`), types counter, gauge, histogram; and **PromQL** for queries like `rate(http_requests_total[5m])`.

Config: `prometheus.yml` lists scrape targets (the app, Node Exporter, other services); in AWS use EC2 service discovery or static targets in Compose.

Why host metrics matter for LLM apps: they show saturation (memory leaks, disk full, file descriptors) but are secondary to application metrics. Retention is local and limited by disk; for long-term storage use remote write. Failure mode: high-cardinality labels (per user id) exploding memory.

Observe infrastructure (Prometheus, Node Exporter) and the app (requests, p95, errors, tokens, blocks). Grafana next to quality. Alert only what needs a human. Trace in Langfuse. Sample online evals. Turn misses into gold cases.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Prometheus & Node Exporter. Run Prometheus to collect metrics from every instance, using Node Exporter for CPU, memory, disk, and network.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, prometheus & Node Exporter is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Week one you watch traffic, errors, tokens, and a weekly sampled review — not twenty pages of unused panels.

The concrete requirement is: Run Prometheus to collect metrics from every instance, using Node Exporter for CPU, memory, disk, and network. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, quality dashboards sit beside SRE; one click from a bad answer to an eval case. A strong answer names this item (Prometheus & Node Exporter) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## What it is

An alert should mean "a human must act now". Everything else belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket queue.

Good alert properties: **symptom-based** (users affected), actionable, has a runbook link, has a sensible severity and is not noisy.

Examples for an LLM service:
- Error rate above X% for 5 minutes.
- p95 TTFT above SLO for 10 minutes.
- Provider 429 rate sustained above threshold.
- Spend rate projecting over daily budget (cost runaway).
- Health check failing / no instances healthy.
- Sudden guardrail block spike or feedback drop.

## What it is

Offline evals check known cases before release; **online evals** check live traffic after release.

Sources of quality signal:
- **User feedback**: thumbs up/down, comments, regenerate clicks, copy actions, abandonment. Cheap but sparse and biased toward extremes.
- **LLM-as-judge on a sample** of production traces (faithfulness, relevance, safety) scored asynchronously and attached to traces.
- **Heuristics**: empty answers, refusals, citation missing, very long outputs.
- **Human review** of a small random and a targeted sample.

Practice: sample (to control judge cost), score asynchronously off the request path, record scores in Langfuse/MLflow with the prompt version, chart rolling averages and alert on drops. Respect privacy: redact PII, follow retention rules.

Limits: judges can be biased and feedback is noisy; calibrate judges against human labels periodically.

Observe infrastructure (Prometheus, Node Exporter) and the app (requests, p95, errors, tokens, blocks). Grafana next to quality. Alert only what needs a human. Trace in Langfuse. Sample online evals. Turn misses into gold cases.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Online evals & user feedback. Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, online evals & user feedback is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Week one you watch traffic, errors, tokens, and a weekly sampled review — not twenty pages of unused panels.

The concrete requirement is: Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, quality dashboards sit beside SRE; one click from a bad answer to an eval case. A strong answer names this item (Online evals & user feedback) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Online evals & user feedback” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them.

Export RED + tokens + blocks. Dashboard: health, traffic, latency, errors, spend, faithfulness. Alerts: error spike, latency budget, spend cap, scale fail. Traces with cost per hop. Feedback → suite.

p95 is fine, faithfulness is not. You open the quality row, click a trace, export the case. A spend alert fires before the invoice. A noisy alert on CPU is deleted.

Write the control in the release notes for m10-9: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “Online evals & user feedback” because the happy path works.** Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them. SRE panels with no quality row.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Alerts that page on everything so nobody comes.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement online evals & user feedback. Traces you cannot turn into a gold case.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Online evals & user feedback: Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them. SRE and quality on one board, traces with cost, online samples, misses back into the suite, week-one focus on traffic, errors, tokens, review. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m10-9. A reviewer asks you to prove “Online evals & user feedback.” You page on error rate, not on a pretty chart. You add one case from a thumbs-down. You show the weekly sample notes. That is observability, not a Grafana theme.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need online evals & user feedback?” Why not alert on every judge dip? Judges noise; use a band and a sample. Why Node Exporter? You still run out of disk while the model is “fine.” Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

llm-specific-incidents.explain:
## What it is

Beyond ordinary outages, LLM systems have characteristic incidents:

- **Quality regression**: answers worse after a prompt, model, retrieval or data change, or silent provider update.
- **Hallucination spike** or citation failure.
- **Cost runaway**: agent loop, giant context, retry storm, abuse.
- **Provider outage or 429 storm**.
- **Latency spike**: long outputs, provider slowdown, retrieval slowness.
- **Prompt injection / data leak** event.
- **Stale or corrupted index**, embedding mismatch after a model change.
- **Guardrail false-positive wave** refusing valid users.
- **Tool side effect**: agent took a wrong action.

Classify severity by user impact, data exposure and spend. Detection comes from alerts, feedback drops and online evals. Knowing the categories lets you pick the right diagnosis path fast. Interview tip: give one example per category and the metric that would reveal it.

The capstone is incidents, levers, runbooks, re-eval on vendor model changes, blameless reviews, and a one-page runbook: prompt id, pin, eval command, who to call. The story is page, roll back, add the miss.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: LLM-specific incidents. Recognize the incidents specific to LLM applications: a provider outage, a silent model update, a prompt regression, a stale index, a runaway agent, and a cost spike.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

## What it is

Once you know the cause, pull the matching lever (fastest, lowest-risk first).

- **Bad prompt version**: move the registry label back.
- **Bad code release**: redeploy the previous SHA tag.
- **Model change/regression**: pin or switch back to the previous model id.
- **Provider outage/429**: fail over to a secondary provider or smaller model, enable cached answers, shed load, tighten rate limiting.
- **Cost runaway**: lower step/token caps, block abusive keys/users, disable the expensive feature via flag.
- **Retrieval/index problem**: switch the index alias to the previous build, trigger reindex.
- **Guardrail false positives**: relax threshold or disable the rule via config.

## What it is

Model changes are releases. Whether you upgrade voluntarily, a provider deprecates a model, or an alias moves, re-run your evaluation before and during the switch.

Process:
1. Track provider deprecation notices and schedule migrations early.
2. Run the **full eval suite** on the candidate model with the current prompts; compare against the baseline per metric and slice, plus cost and latency.
3. Re-tune prompts if needed (a prompt tuned for one model may underperform on another), then re-evaluate.
4. Roll out gradually (canary percentage or shadow traffic comparison), watching online metrics.
5. Keep the old model pinned and available for rollback until stable.
6. Update the baseline.

Also re-evaluate judges: changing the judge model changes scores. Failure mode: switching to a cheaper model on benchmark claims without testing your domain data.
